source.drive: AMAF 2026 (Keynote Address and Official Opening of the Forum)

segments.text: Ladies and gentlemen, please rise if you are able as we welcome our guest of honor and the accompanying delegation. Let's give them a warm welcome. Yes, that's the right energy.
Keep it on, keep it on, keep it on. You may be seated. Good morning.

Honorable Dr. Eva Butera, Minister of State in the Ministry of Health of the Republic of Rwanda and our guest of honor for today. Your Excellency Mridu Pavandas, High Commissioner of the Republic of India to Rwanda. Your Excellency Henrik Nilsson, Ambassador of Kingdom of Sweden to Rwanda.

Ms. Lydia Zigomo, UNFPA Regional Director for Eastern Southern Africa. Dr. Olive Vazirete, Dean of School of Nursing and Midwifery at the University of Rwanda. Representatives of the continental and regional organizations, distinguished midwives, partners, colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, welcome to the Africa Midwifery Acceleration Forum 2026.

Yes, I have the right audience. Now, without further ado, I had promised you to taste a bit of the culture of Rwanda through a dance troupe. Without further ado, a round of applause as we welcome Ndangamirwa cultural troupe, please.

Can you show that to them by a round of applause? Beautiful. Now, ladies and gentlemen, allow me to recognize the presence of the UNICEF Rwanda country representative, Miss Liek van Juheel, who will give us an address on behalf of the UN Residence Coordinator. Thank you for being with us.

I'd also like to welcome and recognize the presence of the UN Women's representative, Mrs. Marie Goretz Ndigama, A round of applause, please. Thank you. How are we feeling so far? Let me get a shout and energy from the room.
No. Yeah. Thank you.
Now, looking around the room, there's one thing we can all agree on. And it's hard for 200 people or more to agree on one thing. But it's for sure one thing we all can agree on.
And guess what that is? It is the fact that we were all born. Anyone disagree? No. And for many of us, when we were born, a midwife was there to welcome us into the world.

We may not remember the introduction, but it was a very important one. And if there was no midwife at your birth, even more reason for you to join this conversation. Because every mother and every child birth deserves skilled care.

So here to say that whether personally or through someone we love, this is a conversation that touches us all. Today, however, we will be discussing of midwifery beyond clinical practice and beyond delivery room. We are discussing its role as an anchor for primary health care supporting women and families and communities throughout their lives.

Over the next three days, we will extend experiences, strengthen partnerships, and agree on practical steps to advance midwifery across Africa. The midwives here today, a special welcome to you. Your experience and leadership are central to this conversation.

Yes, a round of applause for the midwives and midwife leaders. Thank you. Please know that your experience and leadership are central to this conversation and our shared commitment to ending preventable maternal and newborn deaths.
And it is an absolute pleasure to have all of you here. Now, before we proceed, my name is Annette Nizewa. I am the SRHR integration and emerging trends specialist at UNFPA Rwanda.
I can bet on your cheering on, because otherwise, if you don't cheer me on, I might step down. So keep the energy. At the heart of this gathering, ladies and gentlemen, are midwives.

And what better way to start about this conference other than starting with a midwife herself? It is only fitting that we begin hearing from the profession itself. Please join me in welcoming Dr. Olive Valdirete, Dean of School of Nursing and Midwifery at the University of Rwanda. And she will be also representing the Rwanda's midwifery profession.
A round of applause to Dr. Olive until she gets here, please. Dr. Olive, you're welcome. Thank you so much.

Mura Honza, Honorable Minister of Health in Rwanda, the UN Residency Coordinator, the UNFPA Regional Director for East and Southern Africa, Your Excellency, the High Commissioner of India to Rwanda, Your Excellency, the Ambassador of Sweden to Rwanda, Distinguished Representative of the Government of Rwanda, Development Partners, Leaders of Professional Associations, Colleagues, fellow midwives, Ladies and gentlemen, good morning. It's my great honor and privilege to welcome you all to this important Africa Midwifery Accelerator Forum. I warmly welcome our distinguished dignitaries and every participant who has traveled from different corners of Rwanda, from different corners of Africa, and from beyond Africa to join us in this important conversation about the future of midwifery.

Your presence demonstrates our shared commitment to advancing women's health, newborn survival, and a stronger health system. Let me sincerely appreciate the Government of Rwanda, the Minister of Health, UNFPA, Africa CDC, and all partners for making this important gathering possible. Ladies and gentlemen, we meet at a critical moment for Africa.

Despite significant progress, preventable maternal and newborn death remain an acceptable reality in many communities. Yet, we know that midwives are central to changing these situations. Do you agree with me? Midwives are not simply providers of maternal services.

They are skilled professionals, advocates for women's rights, educators, they are counselors and essential contributors to resilient health systems. When well-educated, regulated, adequately supported, and enabled to practice to their full scope, midwives can deliver approximately 90% of essential sexual reproductive, maternal, newborn, and adolescent health interventions. Our midwifery education journey in Rwanda began in 1929 with a training program for medical assistants, followed by assistant midwifery training in 1949, and A2, those holding a secondary education, started in early 1960s.

Following the 1994 genocide against the Tutsi, Rwanda reviewed the health workforce and transformed midwifery education through university-level training. Today, we are graduating midwives with PhD degrees. Our Doctors of Nursing and Midwifery Practice program has opened its doors, and midwives are increasingly advancing into higher academic and professional levels up to professional academic ranks.

This is a remarkable reflection of the country commitment to strengthening the midwifery profession, and thank you so much to the government of Rwanda. Today, Rwanda has grown from one midwifery school to 11 training institutions across the country. This transformation reflected the visionary leadership of our government, supported by the strategic investment and initiatives such as the 4 by 4 health workforce strategy by the Minister of Health.

And the impact is visible. Rwanda maternal mortality ratio has fallen from over 1,000 deaths per 100,000 live births in 2000 to 149 per 100,000 live births today. And this is a significant progress, although our ambition must be to save every preventable life.

Distinguished participants, as we reflect on the central role of midwives in transforming health outcomes, I would like to pose a question. How could we make as a key outcome of this high-level forum to be the establishment and the operationalization of an Africa midwifery hub? Such hub could serve as a continental platform for strengthening midwifery leadership, education, research, innovation, knowledge, exchange and policy advocacy while connecting the countries to accelerate the progress through shared Africa solutions. I hope our discussion will be broad, practical and action-oriented, translating commitment into tangible improvement for women, newborns, families and communities across Africa.
Once again, welcome to Rwanda. Murakaza Neza, Murakozu-Chan. Thank you very much, Dr. Bazirete.

Another round of applause for our speaker, please. Thank you for your remarks and that warm welcome. Now, before we go further, let us take a moment to look at the midwifery accelerator, what brings us together and what we hope to achieve through this forum.

And for that, I am pleased to welcome Frida Temple, comprehensive sexual and reproductive health and rights specialist at UNFCA headquarters to help frame the work ahead. You're welcome, Frida. Good morning, everyone.

I'm a little shorter than... There we go. Honorable Minister of State, honorable UNFCA regional director, all protocols observed. My name is Frida Temple and I work at UNFCA HQ based in Nairobi, where I lead the midwifery acceleration work globally.

So I'm truly excited and honored to stand in front of you in this room today, overlooking the representation spanning the entire African continent. If you look around this room, we have strong midwives, we have the policy makers and we have our continental leadership gathered together with one shared purpose. But we are not starting from scratch.

We already possess overwhelming global evidence providing why midwives are indispensable, backed by a wealth of global and regional data, standards and guidance. This forum brings all of that rigorous evidence together, combining it with the insights we gathered through extensive consultations across every single region of Africa. We're merging all of this knowledge into one unified actionable roadmap built specifically for the African continent.

So our core objective here is clear and ambitious, to achieve continental consensus and high-level commitment around a single evidence-informed roadmap. We're here to agree on the concrete actions that will accelerate midwifery across Africa, spanning leadership, practice, education, regulation, financing and the transition to midwifery models of care. As part of driving this momentum forward, we're also thrilled to mark the launch of the African Midwifery Leadership Network, ensuring that midwives themselves are well-networked and connected and at the forefront of shaping policy and driving change.

Over the course of this forum, we'll hear powerful country and regional evidence and real-world examples. Together, we'll roll up our sleeves to refine, review and validate the Continental Midwifery Acceleration Roadmap. To make it easier for you in this forum, we've developed this QR code that you can see on that slide, leading to a participant guide.

The participant guide includes the agenda, the draft roadmap actions and the link to the resources used. Lastly, to ensure our roadmap translates into real-world impact, it's anchored around a proven strategic advocacy and implementation framework, which is called the Midwifery Accelerator. This was developed in close partnership with our global partners, including WHO, ICM, UNICEF and JPEGO, as well as champion countries such as Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Zambia, and from other regions as well.

This framework focuses squarely on strengthening the midwifery profession and workforce and transitioning to midwifery models of care. The framework is structured around three core pillars and seven targeted accelerators, as you can see on the slide. Each day of the forum will follow one of the pillars, ensuring all of us are able to provide input and expertise to all of the seven accelerators.
We have the right people in the room. Let's harness this momentum and work together to shape the agenda for midwifery acceleration across Africa, from Africa to Africa. Thank you.

Thank you very much, Frida, for setting that background. Please do not be tired when I ask you to give another round of applause to speakers. And I believe that after this presentation, we all have a common understanding of why we are gathered here.

Now, we all know that partnerships become meaningful when shared commitments translate into investments and opportunities that strengthen national capacity. India's support through the India-UN Development Partnership and the Aim for Change initiative has contributed to Rwanda's efforts to advance midwifery. It is now my pleasure to welcome His Excellency Mridul Pavan Das, High Commissioner of the Republic of India to Rwanda, to deliver his remarks.

Your Excellency, you're welcome. Honorable Dr. Ivan Butera, Minister of State and the Minister of Health, Republic of Rwanda, Ms. Lidia Zegomo, Regional Director of the United Nations Population Fund, His Excellency and my dear colleague, Henrik Nielsen, Ambassador of Sweden to Rwanda, Representative of the African Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, Africa CDC, Dr. Oliva Bazirate, Dean, School of Nursing and Midwifery, University of Rwanda, Representatives of the African Union Commission, AUDA, NEPAD and Regional Economic Communities, Chief Midwifery Officers, Leaders of Professional Midwifery Associations and Educators, Distinguished Representatives of Maternal and Newborn Health, Donor Agencies and International Development Partners, Honored Guests, Delegates, Ladies and Gentlemen, Good morning. It is a privilege and joy for me to stand with you today on behalf of the Government of India and this inaugural ceremony of the Africa Midwifery Acceleration Forum 2026.

We meet today in our common pursuit to accomplish a mission that is as compassionate as it is urgent, ensuring that no woman loses her life while giving life and that every newborn is welcomed to the world in safety, health and hope. Midwives are far more than healthcare professionals. They are the heart and soul of resilient health systems.

When midwives are well-educated, respected and fully supported, they deliver 90% of essential sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn and adolescent healthcare. Simply put, supporting midwives saves countless mothers, babies and futures. Yet, across Africa and Asia, workforce gaps and resource constraints far too often stand between mothers and the care they deserve.

This forum is our shared moment to turn bold visions for the African Union Agenda 2063, the Continental Roadmap on Reproductive Maternal and Newborn Child and Adolescent Health 2026-2030, Sustainable Development Goals SDG 3 and SDG 5, and the WHO Regional Committee Africa Health Workforce Agenda into real, lasting action on the ground in every community. Honorable Minister of State Dr. Ivan Dutera, ladies and gentlemen, India's friendship with Africa has always been rooted in South-South solidarity built on trust, deep mutual respect and a shared commitment to uplifting our communities together. We believe that strongest health solutions are created when we walk shoulder-to-shoulder building national institutions and honoring local leadership.

Here in Rwanda, this commitment is brought to life through Government of India's flagship initiative Aim for Change, advancing Rwanda's midwifery to accelerate the realization of zero preventable maternal deaths. Supported by a grant of US$1 million by Government of India through the India-UN Development Partnership Fund, managed by the United Nations Office for South-South Cooperation and brought to fruition with UNFPA Rwanda and the Ministry of Health, this current investment contributes its part to the midwifery ecosystem in Rwanda. Through Aim for Change, our joint efforts are achieving key milestones including funding scholarships for midwifery students, rolling out a standardized national midwifery curriculum and introducing VR simulation tools to enhance clinical training.

I'm happy to note that over the last two years of this ongoing project, 488 students have been trained for advanced diploma, bachelor's and master's programs. The project also promotes faculty development to strengthen training and innovation and capacity building for midwives. In 2026 alone, 338 students received scholarships representing a major positive deviation that significantly exceeded the original annual target of 150.

South-South exchanges with Indian experts and targeted support for the Rwanda Association of Midwives are further strengthening leadership, digital innovation and peer-to-peer learning. These investments directly support Rwanda's 4x4 health workforce strategy to quadruple healthcare staff while advancing our joint goal of zero preventable maternal deaths. Building on the success, India strongly endorses this forum's key outcomes including the Continental Midwifery Acceleration Roadmap 2026-2035 and the Pan-African Midwifery Leadership Network.

To all our development partners, African Union leaders, Africa CDC and civil society, India stands ready to deepen and expand South-South solidarity. Let us join forces to scale up simulation learning, digital technology, domestic health investments and supportive policies so that midwives everywhere can practice with confidence and full support. I extend my heartfelt gratitude to the Ministry of Health of Rwanda, UNFPA, the African Union Commission, Africa CDC and every organizer who made this remarkable gathering possible.

Ladies and gentlemen, midwives do not just deliver babies, they nurture life, hope and the future of our nations. By uplifting them, we build a healthier, brighter future for generations to come. India remains dedicated to walking hand in hand with Rwanda and all our African sister nations toward a world where no mother or child is left behind.
I wish this forum all the best. May it come up with deeply enriching and productive discussions on a mission which connects us all together. Thank you.
Murakoze Chan. Looks like the audience is cooperating and I don't need to say a round of applause again because that was sufficient. Thank you very much.

Thank you, Your Excellency, for your remarks and for India's valued partnership. Now, ladies and gentlemen, this forum also gives us an opportunity to learn from one another across countries. With that in mind, we now turn to Egypt for a video message from His Excellency Professor Dr. Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, Minister of Health and Population of the Arab Republic of Egypt.
Kindly direct your attention to the screen and stay as quiet as possible. Thank you. Wish colleagues, every birth is a defining moment in the lives of women and families.

How we organize care around that moment reflects not only the quality of our health services but also our commitment to protecting the lives and rights of mothers and newborns. In Egypt, with nearly 2 million births every year, improving maternity care is a national priority. Despite progress in maternal and newborn health, high cesarean section rates, variations in service quality and unequal access to safe and respectable care remains important challenges.

We recognize that addressing these challenges requires more than improving individual services. It requires rethinking the model of maternity care itself. This vision is reflected in Egypt's National Midwifery Strategy 2023-2030, which seeks to establish an integrated woman-centered model that promotes normal physiological birth whenever appropriate, ensures continuity of care and guarantees timely access to specialized interventions when needed.

At the heart of this model is effective collaboration between midwives, obstetricians, pediatricians and other health professionals It is not about replacing one profession with another, but about ensuring that each contributes accordingly to their competences to provide the right care for every woman and newborn. To achieve this, Egypt is working toward developing a workforce of 9,000 midwives by 2030, starting with approximately 1,300 trainees and planning to expand by another 7,700. This investment combines competency-based education, clinical training and the development of educators and supervisors alongside professional recognition, licensing and appropriate employment opportunities.

Developing this workforce must go hand in hand with creating an enabling clinical environment. We are strengthening professional regulations, defining scopes of practice and clinical privileges, improving supervision and referral pathways, and promoting respectable maternity care. We are also advancing the use of the Labor Care Guide and the ROPSON classification to improve clinical practices and address unnecessary caesarean sections.

An equally important part of this transformation is extending midwifery services through Egypt's extensive primary health care network, connecting antenatal care with childbirth, postnatal follow-up and family planning. Our ambition is full coverage across the targeted primary health care network, supported by qualified personnel, essential resources and reliable referral systems. For this expansion to be sustainable, midwifery must also become an integral part of health system financing.

Egypt's universal health insurance system offers an opportunity to incorporate appropriate midwifery services into benefit packages and strategic purchasing arrangements. Our international partnership further supports this transformation. Through the collaboration with our friends at the UNFPA and the Burnett Institute, we are strengthening the capacity of midwifery educators, while our partnership with the International Confederation of Midwives supports supervision, educational quality assurance and alignment with international standards.

Distinguished colleagues, ladies and gentlemen, the potential impact of this investment is substantial. Egypt's modeling for accelerated investment during the 2026-2030 projects that scaling up midwifery could avert approximately 259 maternal deaths, more than 26,000 neonatal deaths and over 11,000 child deaths and around 13,600 stillbirths, while preventing approximately 860,000 unintended pregnancies. It also projects cumulative health service savings of approximately 9.7 billion Egyptian pounds.

These are projected rather than achieved outcomes, but that demonstrates the significant health and economic value of investing in midwifery. Midwifery also contributes to health system resilience, and during epidemics and humanitarian emergencies, women continue to give birth, making the continuity of essential maternal and newborn services indispensable. As we look towards 2030, Egypt is committed to making midwifery a recognized, regulated and fully integrated component of its health system.

Ultimately, our success will be measured not only by the number of midwifers we train, but with the quality of care women receive and the lives mothers and newborns will be protected. Our ambition is not simply to revive midwifery in Egypt, it is to make it a driving force in transforming maternity care for generations to come. Anna, thank you.

Our sincere thanks to Professor Abdel Ghaffar for contributing to this forum. If you're here on their behalf, please pass our sincere thanks to them. Now, of course, advancing midwifery takes sustained commitment and investment.

Sweden is a valued partner, supporting this forum and the wider priorities of women's health, gender equality and stronger health systems. On that note, please join me in welcoming His Excellency Henrik Nilsson, Ambassador of the Kingdom of Sweden to Rwanda, to deliver his remarks. Your Excellency, the floor is yours.

Honorable Minister of State, Dr. Yvonne Butera, Distinguished Representatives of UNICEF and UN Women, Dear Olugbemiga Adelakin of UNFPA and the UNFPA leadership, Dear Dr. Oliv Basirete, Dean of University of Rwanda, Dear Excellency High Commissioner of India, Pabandas, Ladies and Gentlemen, Dear Midwives, Good morning. It is a great honor and privilege for me to join you here and to have the opportunity to address this audience during the opening ceremony on behalf of the Embassy of Sweden. Allow me first to express my sincere appreciation to the Government of Rwanda, the African Union Commission, Africa CDC, UNFPA and all partners who have worked tirelessly to convene this landmark forum.

The gathering of more than 200 leaders, policymakers, health professionals, educators and advocates from across Africa sends a powerful message. It demonstrates our shared determination to move towards concrete actions that improve the lives of women, newborns, adolescents and families across the continent. The theme of this forum has excellent timing.

Today we are called not merely to discuss midwifery but to accelerate it. And to translate strategies into investments, policies and services that reach every community. Kigali, a city that has become synonymous with ambition and innovation, is a very good choice for this kind of discussion.

The evidence concerning midwifery is overwhelming. When midwives are educated and trained according to international standards, adequately supported and integrated with functional health systems, they can provide up to 90% of essential sexual, reproductive, maternal, newborn and adolescent health services. They save lives every day.
They ensure safer pregnancies and safer births. They expand access to contraceptives and counseling. They protect newborns during the most vulnerable moments of life.

They support adolescent health. And they serve as trusted advocates for women and families within their communities. To put it differently, there is perhaps no greater investment that countries can make in maternal and newborn health than investments in a strong and empowered midwifery workforce.

However, challenges exist. The reality is that across East and Southern Africa, the region continues to face an estimated shortage exceeding 300,000 midwives. This shortage is compounded by the migration of health workers, uneven distribution between urban and rural areas, difficult working conditions, and growing pressures in humanitarian and fragile settings.

At the same time, the global financing landscape is changing rapidly. External funding remains important, but no health system can depend indefinitely on external resources alone. Strong policies cannot succeed without sustainable financing.

Dedicated health workers cannot deliver services without adequate equipment, medicines, infrastructure, and support. And to achieve the objectives of ambitious roadmaps, domestic ownership and long-term investment are needed. Building resilient health systems will therefore require strong domestic financing, evidence-based investment cases, and sustained commitment.

As we prepare to shape the Continental Midwifery Acceleration Roadmap, allow me to highlight three areas of priority. First, investment. Investments in midwifery must be recognized as a high-return investment in health, human capital, and economic development.

Second, education and deployment. Access to competency-based, degree-level education and modern simulation-based learning must be expanded, and we must strengthen regulatory systems and professional standards. Third, advocacy and empowerment.

The voices of midwives should inform national health policies, workforce planning, education reforms, and strategic investments. The future of healthcare should not simply be designed for midwives, but with midwives. As you have noticed, these three areas of priority correspond very well to the three pillars of this forum.

My country, Sweden, has a longstanding commitment to sexual and reproductive health and rights, gender equality, and universal access to quality healthcare. Women's and adolescents' sexual and reproductive health and rights are fundamental human rights and an integral component of sustainable development. We believe that access to healthcare and SRH services, information, and contraceptives is crucial for any country to achieve inclusive economic growth, social justice, and sustainable development.

We also believe that universal health coverage, bodily autonomy, and gender equality are deeply interconnected. Progress in one area strengthens progress in all other areas. I am therefore very pleased to announce that Sweden is preparing to commence a new and innovative 18-month program implemented by UNFPA in partnership with Medical Doctors for Choice.

The initiative has been specifically designed to strengthen and empower midwives while advancing access to quality rights-based sexual and reproductive health services. It will take place in five African countries, including Rwanda. The program will focus on digitalization, capacity development, and professional development as means to improve service delivery.

It will aim to ensure that future generations of midwives are equipped with the competencies, clinical skills, and leadership capabilities required to respond effectively to modern healthcare challenges. Finally, distinguished delegates, let me underline that Sweden is proud to stand shoulder to shoulder with the African Union, UNFPA, Africa CDC, and all partners committed to advancing maternal and newborn health. We fully support the development of the Continental Midwifery Acceleration Roadmap and welcome its ambition to strengthen leadership, education, regulation, financing, and workforce development across Africa.
Let's seize this moment to transform continental commitments into country action. I wish you all a productive and inspiring forum. Thank you very much.

If you could please give another round of applause to Ms. Ekman. Thank you, Your Excellency, for your remarks and for Sweden's continued support. As we know, strong health systems depend on skilled and supported workforce.

With care available where people need it the most. To bring that continental perspective into our discussion, we will now hear a video from Dr. Jean Casier, the Director of the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Please direct your attention to the screen as we play the video.

Honorable Ministers, my own sister, the ED, UNFPA DNA Cater, dear colleagues and friends, and above all, dear midwives of Africa, I bring you warm greetings from Addis Ababa in Ethiopia. I regret that I cannot join you physically in Kigali, but let me thank the government of Rwanda, UNFPA, and all partners for organizing this important forum, which addresses one of the most urgent and unacceptable challenges facing our continent. According to the latest estimates from WHO, UNICEF, UNFPA, and the World Bank, around 260,000 women died worldwide in 2023 from causes related to pregnancy and childbirth.

Of these, nearly 179,000 were African mothers. This means that our continent accounted for almost 70% of all maternal deaths worldwide. Beyond these figures are mothers who never return home, children who will grow up without their mothers, and families whose lives have been changed forever.
What makes this tragedy particularly unacceptable is that most of these deaths are preventable. We have the scientific knowledge. We know the interventions that work.

Yet we continue to lose mothers and newborns because our health systems are not delivering what they should. At Africa CDC, our recent continental assessment of maternal and child mortality is reinforcing two critical priorities. Improving the quality of care and addressing the shortage of qualified health professionals, particularly midwives.

Across Africa, women continue to die by giving birth without access to skilled care. In some communities, women travel for hours to reach a health facility only to discover that no qualified midwife is available. Yet in those same countries, we have trained midwives who remain unemployed.

How can we explain this? How can government invest in training health professionals and then fail to create positions for them to serve our people? How can we continue discussing maternal mortality while qualified professionals remain at home unable to practice? For us in Africa CDC, this is not simply a technical challenge. It's a question of governance and political responsibility. We must change the way we measure progress.

Training thousands of midwives is not enough. We must know how many are employed, where they are deployed, whether they are paid, and whether they have medicines, equipment, and working conditions to save lives. Let us be clear.

A trained midwife without employment cannot save a mother. And an employed midwife without essential supplies cannot deliver the quality of care that every woman deserves. Excellencies, dear colleagues and friends, let me acknowledge the leadership of Her Excellency Samia Sulu President of Tanzania and AU Champion for Maternal, Newborn, Child, and Adolescent Health.

Her leadership gives us an important opportunity to translate our continental ambitions into concrete national commitment. But political leadership must be accompanied by national budget, functioning health systems, and measurable accountability. This is precisely where Africa CDC intends to strengthen its engagement with Member States, UNFPA, WHO, and all other partners.

Next week, we'll gather in Addis Ababa for CPHIA Conference of Public Health in Africa 2026. If you are in this room today without registration, please let me tell you that already 39,000 people registered. Several heads of state and government confirmed, and almost all global health leaders will attend.

Dear friends, I will also be honest with you as an African. I start to see attacks to Africa CDC because we are organizing this world-class conference. Even I'm told that there are some attacks to our website.
I will not say sorry because Africans can also organize big events. Africans can bring the world. Those who don't respect Africa will become used to us.

In Africa CDC, we don't give up. We'll continue to make this continent proud despite all baseless attacks. I want to invite you to attend the CPHIA where Mama Samia will launch her roadmap for the maternal child health.

And I want this meeting in Kigali to contribute to this roadmap when we'll be in Addis Ababa. We need to ask how many additional midwives we need in Africa. How many trained midwives we need to employ? What financing is requested? How and which government can do to close the gap? Colleagues, Africa CDC is advancing the vision of Africa's security and sovereignty.

Africa cannot claim to have achieved health security and sovereignty while its mothers continue to die from preventable causes during pregnancy and childbirth. Do we have to excuse ourselves because we are pushing this agenda? No. To our midwives today, I want to express my profound respect.

You deserve more than appreciation and recognition. You deserve employment, investment, decent working conditions and a meaningful voice in shaping our health systems. I will be there to continue to talk about it.

To our government, we need the political courage to do what must be done. To our partners, we love our partners. Is there an issue to accept the leadership of a government and to be aligned under this leadership? You saw me a month ago raising my voice when I was looking for 700 million not uncutted for the Ebola response.

Currently, after one month, I have visibility for $820 million. Is it important to raise voice to show more transparency? I don't think so. This is why we are inviting partners to work on more transparent and respectful way with our government.

And we want our government to really lead. I will be more than happy to meet all of you because this conversation will continue next week in Addis Ababa during the CPHA. I wish you successful deliberations and thank you.

Our sincere thanks to Dr. Kaseya. Thank you very much. Now, many of us already know UNFPA's longstanding commitment to investment in midwifery as a pathway to ending preventable maternal and newborn deaths and assuring equality and the quality of care for every woman and newborn.

To share the regional perspective and the priorities ahead, it is my absolute pleasure to welcome Ms. Lydia Zegomo, the Regional Director for Eastern Southern Africa UNFPA. Please, a round of applause as she comes to the stage. Good morning, Your Excellency, the Minister of State for Health in Rwanda, ambassadors of India and Sweden.

The United Nations family, distinguished guests, but most importantly, the champions in the room, the midwives. It's my pleasure to be here this morning with you. And I wanted to thank you for joining us at the Africa Midwifery Acceleration Forum 2026.

It's deeply empowering to stand in Kigali today, surrounded by the true backbone of our health systems and like-minded health leaders from across the continent. I want to extend my profound gratitude to the government of Rwanda, the Ministry of Health, and the Africa CDC for hosting us and for their strategic leadership in establishing a regional midwifery hub. A true beacon of excellence for our continental agenda.

Midwives are at the very heart of UNFPA's programs, interventions, and advocacy. As the United Nations Sexual and Reproductive Health Agency, we're also the population agency and data agency, we know that midwifery is the cornerstone of resilient health systems. They're the critical drivers for improving care for mothers, newborns, and adolescents.

These are not just symbolic statements, they're backed by overwhelming evidence. And a lot of the previous speakers have actually spoken to a lot of what I wanted to say. So, I'm going to have the license of speaking to some real issues that I've seen in my work across East and Southern Africa in particular.

I wanted to actually start by commending the way in which midwives and ministries of health have responded to the needs on the continent. We used to have very silo programming, vertical programs, parallel programs. But increasingly, we're finding that we need to integrate.

Because when a woman or girl comes to a health center, she needs to be seen and seen holistically. As an individual, coming and presenting with different needs and issues and concerns. And so I wanted to commend midwives for the ability they've had to pivot in their profession, to take on board integrated care.

I think in Africa, this is extremely important. In the countries that I visit, and I normally visit 23 countries of East and Southern Africa, from DRC, Ethiopia, Burundi, and Eritrea, all the way down to the islands of Madagascar, Comoros, Seychelles, and Mauritius. And everything in between.

That integrated care means that they're providing not just maternal and newborn and childcare. They're providing support on HIV, which is still a problem in this region. STIs, gender-based violence, and reproductive cancers.

That is a lot. And they're doing that in the communities, not just in the health centers. When I was in DRC in March, and we were in Goma, one of the things that really struck me was the importance of the community-based outreach that midwives take care of.

And that we sometimes don't acknowledge because we think that all things to do with healthcare are happening in static facilities. But actually, in many of our countries, the work is in the community. That is where women at risk, girls at risk, young people at risk are being identified.

That is where the messages that are so important to ensure that the right information is in the hands of those who need it, to make informed decisions about their lives, is taking place. And the one thing that those communities that I met with, including in internally displaced camps, were saying was the importance of the community outreach and how that changed lives and enabled women who had been violated sexually to know that there were safe places they could be directed to the right support, psychosocial, medical, and be accompanied on the journey to recovery. So the work of midwives is extensive.

And investing in care provided by midwives is indeed one of the most effective sustainable strategies available to us. Achieving universal coverage of midwife-delivered interventions by 2035 could avert 67% of maternal deaths, 64% of newborn deaths, and 65% of stillbirths. That equates to saving 4.3 million lives every single year.

Even a 25% increase in coverage every five years will still save 2.2 million lives annually. Yet as we look across Africa, we face profound systemic deficits. Eastern Southern Africa faces an estimated shortage of 307,000 midwives, while North Africa and the Arab region need 128,000 more.

This is compounded by an even distribution, restrictive policy environments, and the acute challenges of fragile and humanitarian settings where midwives are often the sole providers of life-saving care amid disrupted systems. One of the things that really touched my heart this year with Dr. Kaseya's point that he made about the Ebola crisis that is still ravaging the DRC was that the first casualties were health professionals, and some of them, some of our midwives. And it really struck me how this is not just about a job.

This is about someone putting their life on the line for someone else. And we also know from the evidence, I was talking to the WHO Africa director last week at the SADC Health Ministers' Meeting, that actually early intervention with Ebola saves lives. So the more those are infected seek early health care and support, the greater the chances of actually surviving this specific Ebola outbreak.

And the reason so many of them are dying is because they're not going to the health facilities. They're dying, actually 60 plus percent are dying in the community. So midwives have been in that struggle.

We need to see pregnant women still coming to health centers so that they can deliver their children safely. A baby infected by Ebola has hardly any chance of survival, unfortunately. On top of that, I wanted just to touch on something mentioned by one of the earlier speakers that I really wanted to reiterate.

The tragedy that I've seen in some countries of not being able to employ experienced, capable midwives. Midwives. I have visited teaching hospitals in some of my region where the labor wards and maternity wards are staffed by very young, still in training nurses and midwives.

And the number of them as against a trained, licensed, regulated midwife, experienced midwife, did not make sense to me. And I wondered what quality of education these midwives and nurses in training were actually receiving. Yet in that same country, more than 8,000 midwives, trained, experienced midwives, were unemployed.

It left me with a heartache around how we change that injustice. Because it is great that young women, and men in this case, were wanting to enter the profession. But it is a tragedy if the people who could be training them are not actually available in those training hospitals.
Because we're not employing them. It led me to really think that we need to stop seeing midwifery as a voluntary sector. It is life-saving work.

It's national service. Beyond the immediate healthcare benefits, investing in midwife-led care is one of the most profitable investments a government can make for its economic growth and prosperity. So through the midwifery accelerator, UNFPA created an investment case framework to help countries measure the macroeconomic return of training and deploying midwives.

Using this method, we see staggering results. In Zambia, for instance, an investment to achieve 95% universal health coverage through midwives could cost an estimated US$241 million, while yielding economic benefits of US$2.3 billion. This means that for every US$1 invested, Zambia would gain an estimated US$9.3 million in future social and economic benefits, driven by a healthier, better educated, and more productive population.
But beyond the economics, we must look at the day-to-day realities of midwives' work. We all know that midwives save lives. It's clear.

Edna, a 29-year-old midwife in Uganda, recently supported a 23-year-old refugee through the birth of a baby boy at sunrise. Theodora Peter Naki, in Tanzania, successfully resuscitated a newborn who was not breathing, while simultaneously saving the mother from severe postpartum hemorrhaging. Estelle Bahati, in the DRC, treks on foot for over three days to provide family planning and reproductive health care to remote communities in Itula.

While I admire their courage and commitment, I must be candid. I want to see fewer stories of midwives having to perform miracles against all odds. We should not have to rely on women's heroic sacrifice to compensate for fragile systems.

Their life-saving work must be supported, safeguarded, and enabled by robust health infrastructure in every country. A midwife should never have to risk her own safety or exhaust herself beyond human limits to protect the lives of other women. Too many times, I have visited facilities of government and private providers, particularly churches, religious institutions that are operating within the public sphere.

And in the last year, in many of those places, be it Lesotho, Botswana, to Comoros, to Zambia, Zimbabwe, too many times, you enter the facilities, there are competent people waiting to serve, but they don't have the tools they need. They're running out, they're telling you that contraceptives are going to be, have finished within a week. What can we do? That condoms are not available.

I was talking to the Deputy Minister of Health in Botswana last week, and he said, can you help us? We need more condoms. If we don't meet those needs to enable midwives to do their work, we will see what we're seeing, spikes in unintended pregnancies, unsafe abortions, and rising HIV and STI infections, with the resultant cost on national and subnational health systems. So this brings us to our shared purpose over the next three days.

We're here to move from continental commitments to country action. We're here to collaboratively develop the continental midwifery acceleration roadmap for Africa for the period 2026 to 2035, and to establish an African midwifery leadership network. In all countries, midwifery should not be seen as a parallel system to the formal health sector.

It should be part of and integrated within the formal health sector. To achieve this, I kindly and urgently request the leadership and political backing of our ministries of health, our senior government representatives, and our ministers of finance and planning. Let's bring midwives to the center of policy discussions.

Let's ensure their voices are not just heard, but directly incorporated into health policies, workforce planning, and national budget decisions. Let us not have hospitals being built, as I saw. Lovely facility.

But because it was not yet fully equipped with what was required in the maternity ward. The hospital at a lower level that was still serving women, pregnant women, was being seen as substandard. So in this country, women and their husbands were making choices to go to the new facility, not knowing that the new facility was still in transition.

Things were still being set up. When I visited that new hospital, which was indeed still being set up, it was already serving pregnant women. And in one month, the medical superintendent told me, during that transition period, there was a spike in neonatal deaths.

I wondered, who told that grieving mother why her baby died? Who told that grieving father why his baby died? They thought they were choosing a better facility, but they did not know that that better facility was not yet fully set up. We must not let such preventable tragedies happen. If midwives had been involved in the planning for that transition, I wonder would we have seen that spike in neonatal deaths.
So, we have the global position paper on transitioning to midwifery models of care. We have the implementation guidance. We also have the midwifery accelerator as a strategic framework.

Now it's time to materialize these global recommendations into budgeted, accountable national action plans at both the national and subnational levels. As we design, cost, and implement these plans to advance the African Union Agenda 2063 and secure universal health coverage, I'm confident that our proud, skilled midwives will lead the way if we give them that opportunity. So, I hope that's what we're going to do over the next three days.
